newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Dostum forces deploy alongside Masood, draw fire.
newsitem.headline: Dostum forces deploy alongside Masood, draw fire.

text.p: Tanks and troops loyal to northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum reinforced soldiers loyal to the ousted Afghan government between Charikar and the Bagram junction on Thursday and immediately drew fire from Taleban forces, witnesses said.
Dostum insisted that his deployment alongside men loyal to Ahmad Shah Masood, military chief under ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani, did not mean he was spoiling for a fight with the Taleban.
But the Uzbek general now faces a situation where his men are badly exposed unless he takes the fight to the Taleban.
About a dozen of Dostum's tanks and hundreds of his men streamed down from the heights of the Salang Pass through Jabal os-Siraj and on to Charikar on Thursday.

Most deployed on high ground between Charikar and the Bagram junction, at the base of foothills to the west of the main highway, where they overlook Taleban positions around the junction and the Bagram military airbase to the south and east.
As the Dostum elements pulled into position Taleban mortars began pounding their locations, drawing return mortar and artillery fire from Masood's men in the area.
Reporters on the highway south of Charikar late in the afternoon watched the exchange of fire for about an hour with each cracking impact sending smoke and dirt into the sky.
Charikar itself was shuttered and virtually abandoned as residents sought shelter from the nearby shelling and from a fourth straight day of Taleban bombing runs against them.
One bomb landed just five metres (15-feet) from the main highway, leaving a large crater, wounding one man severely and scattering the few persons who had not already fled the area.
The injured man, shopkeeper Ali Akhmed, 65, was taken to Charikar hospital suffering from head, neck and shoulder wounds. He was unconscious and not expected to live.
Dr Abdul Rawuz said Ali Akhmed was one of 11 people wounded in Thursday's fighting in and around Charikar. He said three people had been killed, but his casualty figures were imposssible to verify.
The doctor appealed to the international community for immediate assistance to his abominably filthy hospital.
"Any wounded person who comes here now will surely die because we have not even one medicine," he said.
The town of Jabal os-Siraj, 15 km to the north, was also attacked from the air on Thursday with one bomb falling within a few hundred metres (yards) of reporters in a position north of the town.
Masood's troops, backed by Dostum forces who had just arrived on the scene, let loose with a deafening barrage from a pair of truck-mounted anti-aircraft guns, to no apparent effect.
The situation remained much as was on Monday with troops of the ousted government and Taleban forces battling for control of the Bagram junction about 60 km north of Kabul.
But with Dostum's forces, backed by armour, now inserted in the Masood's line, the Taleban were facing a much stronger foe.
Masood, a Tajik, and Dostum have been rivals and sometime enemies in the years since mujahideen forces entered Kabul and formed a government in 1992.
The threat both now perceive from the Pashtun-dominated, ultra-conservative Islamic Taleban has led them into military cooperation through a recently formed and broadly based Afghan defence council.
Taleban authorities in Kabul said on Thursday they had been assured by Dostum that he would not join in the fighting north of the capital.

The hotly contested Bagram junction is important because it controls traffic north and south on the main highway, also known as the "old road", connecting the capital to northern Afghanistan through the Salang Pass.

The junction also controls access from the south to the Bagram military airfield about 10 km (six miles) to the northeast. There has been fighting around the airfield for the better part of a week with no clear outcome.

A spokesman for Masood confirmed that the Taleban also hold what is known as the "new road" from Kabul to the airfield, which runs parallel to the old road and just to the east, and also the spur which links the two roads at the Bagram junction.
The main road from Kabul north remained open on Thursday but few dared risk the drive through sometimes active combat around Bagram.
